There is a peculiar kind of freedom in being told to write whatever comes to you. It is not the freedom of a wide-open field exactly; it is the freedom of a field with a fence around it, and someone has said, “Go anywhere, but stay inside the fence.” A thousand words is the fence. Or perhaps it is the field. The constraint makes the openness possible. Without a limit, the mind wanders into the fog and sits down. With a limit, it starts walking.

I think about the first sentence. It always pretends to be a beginning, but it is usually the middle of something. Even now, this thought has parents and grandparents, old conversations, half-read books, a screen at midnight, a cup of tea going cold. The first sentence is a door painted on a wall. You walk through it anyway, because what else are you going to do with a door?

Somewhere outside, a car passes. The sound is a soft tear in the evening. A dog answers it, then decides it has done its duty. There is a mosquito in the room that has been avoiding me with great skill. It is a small reminder that I am not only a mind; I am a body, a warm surface, a thing that can be bitten. All day I have been thinking in paragraphs, but the mosquito thinks in blood. Who is more honest?

I once knew a man who collected words. Not in a notebook, not in a dictionary, but in the way he talked. He would use an old-fashioned word like *gossamer* and then look around as if he had released a bird. He liked *crepuscular*. He liked *susurrus*. He said, “There are words that feel like they were made for the inside of a mouth.” I asked him what he meant. He said, “Say *luminous*. Now say *grief*. They use different parts of the tongue. They leave different aftertastes.” I have never forgotten that. I don’t know if it is true, but I know it is useful. It makes language feel less like a tool and more like a place.

A thousand words is not very long. It is a short story that ends before you know the characters’ middle names. It is an essay that has to choose one argument and defend it with only three examples. It is roughly the length of a long voicemail from someone who has missed you. It is enough to say something true, but not enough to say everything true. That is probably good for me. I am prone to saying everything true and ending up with nothing said.

What comes to me now is the image of a boy standing at the edge of a swimming pool with his toes curled over the rough concrete. The water is very blue. The sun is very bright. He is not afraid of drowning exactly; he is afraid of the cold shock, the first second when the body says *no* before it says *yes*. He jumps anyway. That is what writing is like. You stand at the edge of the blank page, and the first sentence is cold. After that you are in it.

There is something I have been meaning to write about: the way ordinary things become precious when you describe them slowly. A spoon on a table. A bus ticket with a crease down the middle. The sound of a neighbor’s television through a wall. If you look at them long enough, they stop being ordinary. A spoon is a small silver boat. A bus ticket is a receipt for a journey you may not remember making. The neighbor’s television is a distant party you were not invited to. This is not a lie. It is just a different kind of attention.

Attention is the whole game. I think that is what I actually believe. Not that writing is about cleverness, or beauty, or even truth exactly. It is about attention. The world is full of things that are happening at the same time, and most of them are asking, very quietly, to be noticed. A cloud changes shape. A person says *anyway* and means something else. A child holds a crayon with their whole fist. If you pay attention, the ordinary becomes strange, and the strange becomes ordinary, and somewhere in that swing back and forth, a sentence is born.

I wonder what I would write if I had only ten words. Probably something like: *I was here. I noticed. I am still listening.* That is not a story, but it is a start. With a hundred words, I might describe the rain. With a thousand, I can have opinions about rain. I can say that rain is not romantic, but the idea of rain is; that real rain is cold and inconvenient and smells like pavement; that the romance is in the shelter, in the decision to stay inside and watch it, in the tea, in the window, in the feeling of being spared.

There is a spider outside the window. It has built a web between the sill and the frame, and it sits in the middle like a tiny punctuation mark. I don’t know what punctuation it would be. A period, probably. A full stop with legs. It has been there for two days. I have not seen it catch anything. I want to tell it that the location is poor, that the traffic is low, that it should try the other side of the window. But I am not a spider, and perhaps the traffic is invisible to me. Perhaps there are whole economies of small winged things happening at dawn. This is what I mean about attention. You look at a spider and suddenly the world is larger.

I am running out of words, which is the point. The page is no longer empty. It has footprints. We have been here for a thousand words. Time to notice something else.

There is a peculiar kind of freedom in being told to write whatever comes to you. It is not the freedom of a wide-open field exactly; it is the freedom of a field with a fence around it, and someone has said, “Go anywhere, but stay inside the fence.” A thousand words is the fence. Or perhaps it is the field. The constraint makes the openness possible. Without a limit, the mind wanders into the fog and sits down. With a limit, it starts walking.

I think about the first sentence. It always pretends to be a beginning, but it is usually the middle of something. Even now, this thought has parents and grandparents, old conversations, half-read books, a screen at midnight, a cup of tea going cold. The first sentence is a door painted on a wall. You walk through it anyway, because what else are you going to do with a door?

Somewhere outside, a car passes. The sound is a soft tear in the evening. A dog answers it, then decides it has done its duty. There is a mosquito in the room that has been avoiding me with great skill. It is a small reminder that I am not only a mind; I am a body, a warm surface, a thing that can be bitten. All day I have been thinking in paragraphs, but the mosquito thinks in blood. Who is more honest?

I once knew a man who collected words. Not in a notebook, not in a dictionary, but in the way he talked. He would use an old-fashioned word like *gossamer* and then look around as if he had released a bird. He liked *crepuscular*. He liked *susurrus*. He said, “There are words that feel like they were made for the inside of a mouth.” I asked him what he meant. He said, “Say *luminous*. Now say *grief*. They use different parts of the tongue. They leave different aftertastes.” I have never forgotten that. I don’t know if it is true, but I know it is useful. It makes language feel less like a tool and more like a place.

A thousand words is not very long. It is a short story that ends before you know the characters’ middle names. It is an essay that has to choose one argument and defend it with only three examples. It is roughly the length of a long voicemail from someone who has missed you. It is enough to say something true, but not enough to say everything true. That is probably good for me. I am prone to saying everything true and ending up with nothing said.

What comes to me now is the image of a boy standing at the edge of a swimming pool with his toes curled over the rough concrete. The water is very blue. The sun is very bright. He is not afraid of drowning exactly; he is afraid of the cold shock, the first second when the body says *no* before it says *yes*. He jumps anyway. That is what writing is like. You stand at the edge of the blank page, and the first sentence is cold. After that you are in it.

There is something I have been meaning to write about: the way ordinary things become precious when you describe them slowly. A spoon on a table. A bus ticket with a crease down the middle. The sound of a neighbor’s television through a wall. If you look at them long enough, they stop being ordinary. A spoon is a small silver boat. A bus ticket is a receipt for a journey you may not remember making. The neighbor’s television is a distant party you were not invited to. This is not a lie. It is just a different kind of attention.

Attention is the whole game. I think that is what I actually believe. Not that writing is about cleverness, or beauty, or even truth exactly. It is about attention. The world is full of things that are happening at the same time, and most of them are asking, very quietly, to be noticed. A cloud changes shape. A person says *anyway* and means something else. A child holds a crayon with their whole fist. If you pay attention, the ordinary becomes strange, and the strange becomes ordinary, and somewhere in that swing back and forth, a sentence is born.

I wonder what I would write if I had only ten words. Probably something like: *I was here. I noticed. I am still listening.* That is not a story, but it is a start. With a hundred words, I might describe the rain. With a thousand, I can have opinions about rain. I can say that rain is not romantic, but the idea of rain is; that real rain is cold and inconvenient and smells like pavement; that the romance is in the shelter, in the decision to stay inside and watch it, in the tea, in the window, in the feeling of being spared.

There is a spider outside the window. It has built a web between the sill and the frame, and it sits in the middle like a tiny punctuation mark. I don’t know what punctuation it would be. A period, probably. A full stop with legs. It has been there for two days. I have not seen it catch anything. I want to tell it that the location is poor, that the traffic is low, that it should try the other side of the window. But I am not a spider, and perhaps the traffic is invisible to me. Perhaps there are whole economies of small winged things happening at dawn. This is what I mean about attention. You look at a spider and suddenly the world is larger.

I am running out of words, which is the point. The fence is getting closer. I could try to be profound, but profundity is a trap. Better to end honestly. Here is what comes to me at the end: the page is not empty anymore. It has been walked on. There are footprints. Some are mine, some are the reader’s, some belong to the mosquito and the spider and the man who collected words and the boy at the edge of the pool. We have all been here for a thousand words. The water was cold at first. Now it is just water. And it is time to climb out, dripping, and go find something else to notice.
